title: How an RBA Board member weighs the cost of bringing inflation back to target
summary: Renée Fry-McKibbin described a decision in which two policymakers could agree on where inflation should end up and still disagree about the cash rate today. The objective she set out was the midpoint of Australia’s 2–3 per cent inflation target. The difficult choice is how quickly to return there when reducing demand can also cost jobs. She spoke in her personal capacity as a Monetary Policy Board member. In the accompanying discussion she explained that the Bank reports vote counts and keeps individual reasoning confidential. The speech therefore gives a way to interpret a split vote without revealing which way she voted.

Two exhibits put the trade-off in historical context. Year-ended inflation has averaged around the target band during the inflation-targeting period, but had risen back above it in the latest year. Employment as a share of the population had eased from its recent peak and remained high historically. Neither chart determines how many jobs a particular rate rise would cost. Participation can change the employment ratio, and aggregate inflation can combine a sharp energy shock with pockets of excess domestic demand. The immediate difficulty she identified was precisely that combination of strong spending in some parts of Australia, weakness in others and a large external oil supply shock.

Fry-McKibbin’s example of how to make a decision under those conditions was the May Statement on Monetary Policy. After the Middle East conflict began, staff published a baseline and two adverse scenarios. The relevant comparison is how inflation and employment fare when a policy judged suitable in the baseline meets a more persistent shock. If the costs are concentrated among people with little room to adjust, a seemingly modest difference between central forecasts can conceal an important difference between policies. She cited a community survey in which 70 per cent of Australians identified inflation as a key economic concern. That measures its salience. It cannot tell a policymaker how the same respondents would weigh a specific increase in unemployment.

One research programme changes what the Board can know before an official statistical release. Bank researchers developed a tool that can search and aggregate information from roughly 22,000 confidential business interactions over 25 years within the RBA’s secure systems. Firms can discuss their next wage round or hiring decision before it appears in a national release. Adding liaison indicators improved model-based nowcasts for variables including wage growth in the research she described. The speech gives no numerical estimate of that improvement, and the interviews are confidential. A market economist using public surveys would need a separate test of whether those surveys share the same lead.

During questions, Fry-McKibbin drew a precise distinction in response to a question on announced job cuts. She personally values liaison because it reveals intentions and conditions ahead of GDP, inflation and unemployment releases. Staff produce the forecasts. She did not infer a change in the employment outlook from the job-cut announcements or disclose an adjustment to a staff forecast. She also defended post-decision press conferences on unchanged-rate days, when the choice to wait can itself require explanation. Together those remarks suggest how to interpret a Board member’s public engagement: extract information about the evidence members look for, and use the official collective decision for the policy conclusion.

questions.question: Under which oil scenario does delaying disinflation materially protect employment?
questions.detail: Keep the policy alternatives and initial conditions common across scenarios. Vary the persistence of the oil shock and the size of domestic pass-through. Compare both the time spent above target and cumulative employment losses, including their concentration across industries. A ranking that reverses with a small change in persistence would reveal exactly where judgment enters the choice.

questions.question: Does business liaison improve the wage forecast when assessed only with information available on the day?
questions.detail: Compare a model using published labour data with one adding a contemporaneous liaison indicator, on identical forecast dates. Separate wages already negotiated from planned awards, check performance around labour-market turning points, and score the forecasts against both first releases and subsequent revisions. The reported aggregate improvement leaves open which industries or phases account for the gain.

questions.question: Which sign of labour-market weakness would outweigh a still-high employment ratio?
questions.detail: Track hiring intentions, vacancies and hours worked alongside employment relative to population, with separate results for sectors exposed to higher energy costs. Job losses at a handful of prominent firms can coexist with hiring elsewhere. A sustained decline in hours and recruitment across sectors would carry more information about future employment than announcements concentrated in one industry.

questions.question: What can a split vote tell us about the next decision?
questions.detail: Compare the published vote counts with successive collective explanations of uncertainty about inflation persistence and the cost to employment. Count a change in those stated risks as evidence. Individual speeches can clarify the decision members face, but assigning an undisclosed vote to a member would create a misleading history of policy preferences.
